name: Manifest destiny
info: Manifest destiny was the belief, named in 1845, that American settlers were destined to expand westward across North America; it shaped the annexation of Texas, the Oregon and Mexican cessions and the removal of Native peoples.

facts.thinkers: John O’Sullivan, the newspaper man credited by most historians with coining the term in 1845; Jane Cazneau, whom some historians suggest wrote the unsigned editorial in which it first appeared; Thomas Jefferson, whose Louisiana Purchase set the stage for continental expansion; John Quincy Adams, an early proponent of continentalism; Andrew Jackson, who spoke of “extending the area of freedom”; James K. Polk, president during the Oregon and Mexican settlements; Josiah Strong, whose 1885 book revived the idea; Albert J. Beveridge, who defended the acquisitions of 1898
facts.texts: John O’Sullivan’s 1839 article predicting a “divine destiny” for the United States; his essay “Annexation” in the Democratic Review (1845) and his editorial in the New York Morning News (27 December 1845); Thomas Paine’s Common Sense (1776); John Quincy Adams’s letter to his father (1811); Josiah Strong’s Our Country (1885); the historians Frederick Merk’s Manifest Destiny and Mission in American History (1963) and Reginald Horsman’s Race and Manifest Destiny (1981)
facts.ideas: the unique moral virtue of the United States; a mission to spread republican government and the American way of life; a divinely ordained destiny; continentalism, the expectation that one nation would fill North America; Anglo-Saxon racial predominance; the Monroe Doctrine’s warning to Europe; Native peoples expected to assimilate, move or vanish
facts.today: The phrase declined in use after the turn of the 20th century. Wilson used it in 1920 for a mission to lead the cause of democracy, and critics of United States foreign policy use it for interventions abroad. In 2025 Donald Trump used it in an inaugural address, the first president to do so in one.

t: The phrase was coined in 1845 by John O’Sullivan, or, some historians suggest, by Jane Cazneau; it became popular only after Whig opponents of the Polk administration criticised it.

There was never a set of principles defining manifest destiny: it was always a general idea, and its proponents held divergent and sometimes conflicting views, from territorial conquest to the call of a nation setting an example.

It was bound up with the annexation of Texas, the Oregon boundary and the Mexican–American War, and with the removal of Native Americans from their land; critics at the time and since have condemned it as a justification of dispossession.
dyk: John O’Sullivan’s original idea was not a call for expansion by force: he expected Americans to settle new regions, set up democratic governments and then ask for admission to the Union, as Texas had done, and he predicted that even Canada would one day ask.
ev: The Louisiana Purchase doubles the size of the United States
The Transcontinental Treaty transfers Florida from Spain and extends the United States border with Spanish Mexico to the Pacific
Andrew Jackson signs the Indian Removal Act
John O’Sullivan uses the phrase “manifest destiny” in the Democratic Review, and the United States annexes Texas
The Oregon Treaty divides the Oregon Country along the 49th parallel, and the Mexican–American War begins
The Mexican Cession adds Alta California and Nuevo México to the United States
The Homestead Act offers western land to settlers for almost nothing
William McKinley annexes Hawaii and the Spanish–American War brings the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam

sections.origins:
Manifest destiny was the expansionist belief in the 19th-century United States that American settlers were destined to expand westward across North America, and that this destiny was both obvious (“manifest”) and certain. It is rooted in American exceptionalism, romantic nationalism, Anglo-Saxonism and nascent ideas of white chauvinism. The first of its themes, the unique virtue of the United States, was often traced to the Puritan heritage and John Winthrop’s “City upon a Hill” sermon of 1630, and Thomas Paine echoed it in Common Sense in 1776, writing that “we have it in our power to begin the world over again”.

Thomas Jefferson looked forward to a time when the nation’s “rapid multiplication” would “cover the whole northern, if not the southern continent”, and the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 set the stage for continental expansion. John Quincy Adams wrote to his father in 1811 that North America seemed “destined by Divine Providence to be peopled by one nation”. As secretary of state he orchestrated the Treaty of 1818, negotiated the Transcontinental Treaty of 1819 and formulated the Monroe Doctrine of 1823.

Most historians credit the newspaper editor John O’Sullivan with coining the term in 1845, in an essay titled “Annexation” in the Democratic Review urging the annexation of Texas; some suggest instead that the unsigned editorial was written by the journalist Jane Cazneau. His second use, on 27 December 1845, claimed the whole of Oregon.
sections.ideas:
Manifest destiny was never a set of principles; it was a general idea, ill-defined but keenly felt. The historian William Earl Weeks names three tenets: the unique moral virtue of the United States, a mission to redeem the world by spreading republican government and the “American way of life”, and faith in a divinely ordained destiny to succeed in that mission. Proponents offered divergent or conflicting views. Many writers concentrated on expansion into Mexico or across the Pacific, while others took the term as a call to example. Ernest Lee Tuveson wrote that the “vast complex of ideas, policies, and actions” under the phrase were “not, as we should expect, all compatible”.

O’Sullivan saw manifest destiny as a moral ideal, a “higher law”, that overruled other claims. He believed that expansion would happen without the government or the army: Americans would immigrate, set up democratic governments and seek admission to the Union. Continentalism, the belief that the nation would eventually fill North America, was one strand; the Monroe Doctrine was another, and the historian Walter McDougall calls manifest destiny a corollary of it, since expansion was needed to enforce it. Trade with China and Asia was a further motive.

Racial ideas also played a part. The historian Reginald Horsman wrote that a view of the Anglo-Saxon race as innately superior held that “inferior races were doomed to subordinate status or extinction”, and that it was used to justify the enslavement of Black people and the expulsion and possible extermination of Indians.
sections.spread:
The phrase is most associated with the territorial expansion of the United States from 1803 to 1900, though some scholars limit the age of manifest destiny to the continental expansion from the Louisiana Purchase to the purchase of Alaska in 1867. In the 1840s it took the form of calls for “All Oregon” and, after the Mexican–American War began in 1846, for “All Mexico”. Slogans such as “Fifty-four forty or fight” expressed the first. Polk instead renewed an offer to divide Oregon along the 49th parallel, and the Oregon Treaty of 1846 settled it that way.

After 1848 the disagreement over slavery made further annexation by conquest too divisive to be official policy, and the most radical advocates turned to filibustering, private military expeditions. William Walker in Nicaragua and Narciso López in Cuba were the best known; the Democratic national platform endorsed Walker’s expedition. The Ostend Manifesto of 1854, which argued that the United States could seize Cuba by force, effectively killed the effort to acquire it.

After the Civil War the idea revived. Josiah Strong’s Our Country (1885) argued that the future fell to America, and the Republican platform of 1892 spoke of “the manifest destiny of the Republic in its broadest sense”. In 1898 William McKinley said of Hawaii, “It is manifest destiny.” Historians have disagreed whether the acquisitions of the 1890s extended manifest destiny across the Pacific or were its antithesis and merely imperialism.
sections.power:
Democrats used the concept to justify the Oregon claim and the annexation of Texas in 1845 as a slave state, which led to the Mexican–American War in 1846. The war ended with the Mexican Cession, which added Alta California and Nuevo México to the United States. Ulysses S. Grant, who served in it, called it “one of the most unjust ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation”.

The consequences for Native Americans were serious, since continental expansion implicitly meant the occupation and annexation of their land. The federal government bought land through treaties, and its policy was that Indians should join American society and become “civilized”. Thomas Jefferson believed they had to assimilate or be pushed aside, and the historian Jeffrey Ostler holds that he advocated extermination once he thought assimilation was no longer possible. Andrew Jackson signed the Indian Removal Act in 1830. After the Civil War the army waged wars on “non-treaty Indians”, and the Homestead Act of 1862 in some areas resulted in the direct removal of Indigenous communities. Hunting reduced the bison to a few hundred. Francis Parkman wrote in 1851 that Indians were “destined to melt and vanish”.

In 1898 the Spanish–American War brought the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Guam under United States rule. The Philippine–American War followed in 1899, against a revolutionary government that sought independence. These islands were acquired as colonies rather than prospective states, a step validated by the Insular Cases.
sections.critiques:
Opposition began at once. The Whigs denounced the doctrine, one resolution calling its supporters traitors to the Constitution for “preaching the doctrine of the right of conquest”. Robert Winthrop was the first to use the phrase in Congress, on 3 January 1846, mocking “the right of our manifest destiny” and beginning a long line of critics who argued that its advocates cited Providence for actions driven by chauvinism and self-interest. John Quincy Adams repudiated expansionism by 1843 because it meant extending slavery into Texas. Abraham Lincoln opposed the Mexican war and the imperialism of manifest destiny as unjust.

John C. Calhoun opposed annexing all of Mexico on racial grounds: “Ours, sir, is the Government of a white race.” The debate showed a contradiction. The mission suggested Mexicans would be improved by joining American democracy, while racial ideas held that non-whites were unfit to be Americans. Some proponents of annexing all of Mexico regarded it as an anti-slavery measure.

Frederick Merk argued in 1963 that manifest destiny had less support than historians portrayed, and that aggressive continentalism was an aberration backed by a minority. Critics have condemned it as an ideology used to justify the dispossession of and genocide against Indigenous peoples. Two Native American writers, Nick Estes and Tonya Gonnella Frichner, link it to the Doctrine of Christian Discovery. William Jennings Bryan, opposing the Philippine war, wrote that “‘Destiny’ is not as manifest as it was a few weeks ago.”
sections.legacy:
After the turn of the 20th century the phrase declined in use as territorial expansion stopped being promoted as part of America’s destiny. Theodore Roosevelt’s corollary to the Monroe Doctrine in 1904 defined the nation as an “international police power” in the Western Hemisphere and explicitly rejected territorial expansion, so that interventionism replaced expansionism. President Wilson tried to redefine the phrase on a worldwide scale; in 1920 he called it “the manifest destiny of the United States to lead” in making democracy prevail, the only time a president had used it in an annual message.

The belief in an American mission to promote and defend democracy, expounded by Jefferson and continued by Lincoln, Wilson and George W. Bush, still influences American political ideology. Critics of United States foreign policy use “manifest destiny” for interventions in the Middle East and elsewhere, while scholars at the end of the 20th century devised the more positive-sounding “nation building”.

Adolf Hitler and Nazi ideologues studied American westward expansion, including its legal techniques of land seizure and population displacement, as a model for their conquest and ethnic cleansing in Eastern Europe, and the idea directly inspired the concept of Lebensraum. The Empire of Japan adopted the phrase to justify its own expansion; Iris Chang wrote that China was twentieth-century Japan’s manifest destiny. In 2025 Donald Trump used the phrase in his inaugural address.

summary: Manifest destiny was the belief, named in 1845, that American settlers were destined to expand westward across North America. It was never a fixed doctrine, and it shaped the annexation of Texas, the Oregon and Mexican settlements and the removal of Native peoples, while Whigs, Lincoln and later critics condemned it as a cover for conquest and dispossession.
references: Frederick Merk and Lois Bannister Merk, Manifest Destiny and Mission in American History: A Reinterpretation (Harvard University Press, 1995)
Reginald Horsman, Race and Manifest Destiny: The Origins of American Racial Anglo-Saxonism (Harvard University Press, 1981)
David Stephen Heidler and Jeanne T. Heidler, Manifest Destiny (Greenwood Press, 2003)
Michael A. Morrison, Slavery and the American West: The Eclipse of Manifest Destiny and the Coming of the Civil War (University of North Carolina Press, 1999)
Robert E. May, Manifest Destiny’s Underworld: Filibustering in Antebellum America (University of North Carolina Press, 2002)
notes: end 1900 (endCirca true): the article calls the phrase most associated with expansion 1803 to 1900 and says its use declined after the turn of the century; it also notes later uses (Wilson 1920, Japan, Trump 2025) and that the mission idea persists, so end is a judgement. Start 1845 is the coining of the term; the ideas are older (Jefferson, Adams 1811).

The article gives no death toll for Native Americans or for the Mexican–American War, and no figures for the Philippine–American War; none written. The Homestead Act figures (600,000 families, 200 million claims, 270 million acres) conflict in scale with each other, so I left them out. 'Reduced to a few hundreds' for bison is the article's own wording.
Authorship of the 1845 'Annexation' editorial is disputed (O'Sullivan vs Jane Cazneau); both given. The article calls the 27 December 1845 piece O'Sullivan's second use, in the New York Morning News.

The Nazi Lebensraum and Japanese claims are stated flatly in the article's legacy section without attribution to a named scholar; I wrote them as the article does for Nazi Germany, but the editor may want a second source. The Japan claim is attributed through Iris Chang.
The article says Jefferson's use of the Doctrine of Discovery is called 'aka Manifest destiny' by Robert J. Miller; I left that equation out as it is a loose identification.

Left out: Frances Fuller Victor's 1869 essay, the poem 'Filibustering Ethics', American Samoa details, the Bent, St. Vrain case study, the transcontinental railroad and Dina Gilio-Whitaker/Boyd Cothran passages, the 2025 homeland-security post, the Teller and Platt amendments, 20th-century status reforms of Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

Quoted phrases follow the article: 'extending the area of freedom' (Jackson) is in the article but not used in the text; the Whig resolution is quoted from the article as 'preaching the doctrine of the right of conquest'.
